segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What was to be able, can in the to form?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, we have poder. If we want to make could, we have two different coulds. We have a could that refers to the past: I couldn't do it yesterday. And we have a could that refers to the future: but I could do it tomorrow. This future could we learned it already from to be able, would be able: poder, podería, and the e fell out, podría.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: If we want to say I could in the past, most of the time we will probably find ourselves using this line past that we learned, the past that we make with -aba for -ar verbs and -ía for -er/-ir verbs. So, how would you say I could, referring to past? I could, I was able to.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Podía. So, this is I was able to, I could. The past could, podía. We could?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. I couldn't do it because I didn't have the time. For both of these, we can use that line in the past, that ongoing past, even though we're not using it in English. I couldn't do it because I didn't have the time. So, the first bit is: I couldn't do it.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. No podía hacerlo porque no tenía el tiempo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, we're going to contrast much more how we use this line and this dot in the past when we look at that dot. So, what we're seeing for now, even though we haven't looked at the dot yet, that the decisions that we need to make in Spanish about whether we will use this line in the past, this ongoing past, or this dot, this point in the past, is a decision based on context rather than identifying which one we're using in English and then translating it. So, we can begin to look at that even before we've learned the dot in the past.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The word for yesterday was ayer. Ayer.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So, how would you say: I couldn't do it yesterday?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. No podía hacerlo ayer. And when we learn the dot form of the past, we will see that we could have used that one as well. Sometimes they're interchangeable.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Sometimes this dot and this line form are not interchangeable. For example, if we want to use haber to say I had eaten rather than I have eaten, I had gone already rather than I have gone, then we always use the line in the past, always. So, from haber, how do you say I had?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Había. Good. So, if you want to say I had eaten, how would you say it?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: You have a version of the verb that comes after haber no matter what version of haber we have: había, habría, he... Doesn't matter.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Había comido. The word for already in Spanish is ya. Y-a, ya.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And it tends to go at the beginning. That would be the least emphatic place, the most natural place. So, how would you say I had eaten already?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Ya había comido. So, you could say: He wanted to dine with me, but I had dined already. So, he wanted... What is to want?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Querer. So, he wanted... Again we're using the line in the past, because even though in English there we're using the dot, we're not saying he was wanting, he used to want, with querer, we can use the line without any problem because most of the time when you want something, it's not just for an instant. It's kind of an ongoing feeling. The dinner was la cena. What was to dine or to have dinner?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes. He wanted to dine with me?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And this was a bit of an exception. You don't say con mí, you say...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Quería cenar conmigo. But I had already had dinner, I had dined already?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. But if you say quería cenar conmigo pero ya había cenado, I might understand he wanted to dine with me, but he had dined already, no? Because we have the same verb form. So, how would we make that clearer?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Just saying yo at some point?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Exactly. But where? So, give it to me again. And and we can say the word for he as well. Especially when we are contrasting between two people, we will have the habit of putting who. So: He wanted to dine with me, but I had dined already.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Él quería cenar conmigo, pero yo ya había...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What you want to translate not is dined. You want to find the version after haber. This is going to save you a lot of pain.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. He wanted to have dinner with me, but I had already had dinner: Él quería cenar conmigo, pero yo ya había cenado.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now, we don't need to look at or discuss when we use had as opposed to when we use have, when we use I had lost it as opposed to I have lost it, because it's exactly the same in Spanish as it is in English. So, you will just translate the thought, let's say. For example, you might want to say: He was looking for it because I had lost it. He was looking for it because I had lost it. To look for is buscar. Buscar, to look for.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Buscar, to look for. So: He was looking for it, he was searching for it?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. He was looking for it?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Lo buscaba or él lo buscaba porque yo lo había perdido. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say: I would have lost it? So, not I had lost it, I would have lost it.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. I would have lost it: lo habría perdido. Now, I'm not sure if you said habría or habería, because this irregularity that we have, which is habría, happens so naturally because that e kind of falls out, so naturally I think you said habería, but you kind of didn't pronounce the e well, is that right?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: I I meant to say habería, yeah.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes. So, you see even naturally it's happening that e of haber is falling away, and that has been formalized in Spanish. You write it like this: h-a-b-r-i-a, habría. Only with a few verbs this contraction is occurring. Habría. Lo habría perdido, I would have lost it. How would you say I would have got lost, or I would have lost myself?
